newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila Central Bank cut signals lower rates.
newsitem.headline: Manila Central Bank cut signals lower rates.

text.p: Two cuts in Philippine overnight borrowing rates last week have paved the way for a likely fall in interest rates at Monday's treasury bills auction and sparked debate over any impact on the peso, analysts said.
On Friday, the Central Bank cuts its overnight borrowing rate by 0.25 percentage points to 10 percent, three days after cutting rates by 0.1875 percentage points.
The two cuts within the week led to predictions the 91-day treasury bill yield could fall to single digits from the previous 10.159 percent.
A Reuters poll of six banks on Friday showed the market expected the benchmark T-bill yield to decline to 9.917 percent, the lowest since July 1995 when it fell to 9.96 percent.

"There's room for interest rates to go down further since inflation is under control, the exchange rate is stable and the economy is still vibrant. It's not overheating right now," said Paul Joseph Garcia, an economist of Metrobank.
But can the peso withstand a further reduction in short-term rates ?
"Unequivocally, we are getting out," a foreign bank dealer with a large portfolio fund said.
"I don't care whether the peso is stable or not. There are no dues left. For the risk we take, we should get a reasonable return. I'm taking a vacation," he said.
Traders said the peso, based on the 91-day rate, is only yielding a net 2.375 percentage-point premium over the U.S. dollar.

But on the other hand, the peso could be bolstered by the expected large inflows from Europeso issuances and overseas borrowings of companies such as Philippine Long Distance Telephone Co and J.G. Summit Holdings Inc.

"We continue to view the peso positively. The peso has shown strength and stability reflecting the overall progress of the economy and markets and the increasingly positive opinion by foreign investors," Gerard Chase, co-head of global markets at Deutsche Bank, told Reuters from Singapore.
Deutsche Bank is the underwriter of a three billion peso Europeso bond issue by the World Bank.
The peso ended weaker on Friday at 26.334 from the previous close of 26.323.
Traders said the Central Bank's two successive cuts in overnight rates were unavoidable because excessive peso liquidity had softened money market rates.
The increased liquidity of the Philippine currency was attributed to banks desisting from investing after a recent rule imposing a 20 percent tax on term reverse repos.
So far, the Central Bank has managed to stave off major fluctuations in the peso by intervening when needed.
Armed with gross international reserves, which recently reached a record $12.05 billion, the Central Bank has so far been a net buyer of dollars.
Analysts said the Central Bank's dollar buying could eventually backfire since this will further heighten liquidity in the system and may eventually cause peso speculation.
"They don't have the ammunition to control liquidity," said Emma Pante, economist of Far East Bank.
